title: Characteristics of life and classification
blurb: Name the characteristics of living things, order the levels of organization, and classify organisms by domain, kingdom and binomial name.
question: A student finds a mushroom, a moss and a jar of baker's yeast on a field trip. Which of them are autotrophs, which kingdom does each belong to, and how should the scientific name of the yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, be written?

teach.body: Formal definition: living things are made of one or more cells, show order, reproduce, grow and develop, use energy (metabolism), respond to stimuli, maintain homeostasis and, as populations, adapt and evolve, with heredity based on DNA. Plain English: a living thing is built from cells, runs on energy, keeps its inside steady, reacts to its world and makes more of itself. A crystal can grow, and a sponge can soak up water, but neither is made of cells or runs a metabolism.

head: Characteristic
What it means
Example
rows: Made of one or more cells
teach.caption: Textbooks list six to eight characteristics. Learn what each one means; the exam will not hinge on an exact count.

teach.h: From one organism to the biosphere

steps.label: Community
steps.sub: All the populations in an area

teach.caption: Inside the organism the levels run atom, molecule, organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system.

teach.body: Taxonomy sorts organisms into nested groups from broadest to most specific: domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. A species is a group whose members can interbreed and produce fertile offspring. Linnaeus gave each species a two-part (binomial) name, Genus species: the genus is capitalized, the species name is lowercase, and both are italicized in print (underlined by hand), as in Homo sapiens. Organisms that share a genus are more alike than organisms that share only an order.

children.label: Archaea
children.sub: Prokaryotes; often extreme habitats; no peptidoglycan

teach.caption: Viruses are not made of cells, so they sit outside the three domains. "Monera" is an obsolete group, now split into Bacteria and Archaea.

head: Kingdom
Cells
Food
Cell wall
teach.caption: Schemes count five, six or more kingdoms. An autotroph makes its own food; a heterotroph eats or absorbs other organisms.

teach.h: Worked scenario: Jasmine sorts her field-trip finds
teach.body: Jasmine, a pre-nursing student, sorts a moss, a mushroom and baker's yeast. The moss has chlorophyll and cellulose walls: kingdom Plantae, an autotroph. The mushroom and yeast absorb their food and have chitin walls: kingdom Fungi, both heterotrophs, even though the mushroom grows from soil like a plant. All three have nuclei, so all are in domain Eukarya. In her report she types the yeast's name as Saccharomyces cerevisiae, in italics, with only the genus capitalized.

teach.text: Classic slips: class comes BEFORE order, and order before family; the species name is lowercase (Homo sapiens, not Homo Sapiens); fungi are NOT plants (heterotrophs with chitin walls); a population is ONE species, a community is MANY; an ecosystem includes the NONLIVING environment; viruses are not cells and are not a kingdom.

items: Life: cells, order, reproduction, growth, energy use, response, homeostasis, heredity and evolution.
Organism, population, community, ecosystem, biosphere (smallest to largest).
Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species (Dear King Philip Came Over For Good Soup).
Binomial name: Genus species, genus capitalized, both italicized.
Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea (both prokaryotes), Eukarya (protists, fungi, plants, animals).
Autotrophs make food (plants, algae); heterotrophs eat or absorb it (animals, fungi).

summary: You can now list the characteristics of living things, put the levels of organization from organism to biosphere in order, and rank the classification levels from domain to species. You can also write a binomial name correctly and place an organism in its domain and kingdom.

A.q: Which level of organization includes all the populations of different species living in one area?
A.why: A community is all the populations of different species living and interacting in one area.

whyNot.0: An ecosystem is a community PLUS its nonliving environment (soil, water, climate).
whyNot.2: A population is a single species in an area, not all the species together.
whyNot.3: The biosphere is every ecosystem on Earth, far broader than one area.

A.q: Which classification level sits directly above genus in the hierarchy?
A.why: The hierarchy runs order, family, genus, species, so family sits directly above genus.

whyNot.1: Order is above family, two levels above genus.
whyNot.2: Species is below genus, the most specific level.
whyNot.3: Class is above order, three levels above genus.

A.q: Which is the correct way to print the scientific name of the house cat?
A.why: A binomial name is Genus species: genus capitalized, species lowercase, both italicized in print.

whyNot.0: The species name (catus) is written in lowercase.
whyNot.1: The genus name (Felis) must be capitalized.
whyNot.3: Printed scientific names are italicized, not written in plain type.

B.q: An organism has cells with nuclei and chitin cell walls, and it absorbs food from dead leaves. To which kingdom does it belong?
B.why: Fungi are eukaryotic heterotrophs that absorb their food and have cell walls made of chitin.

whyNot.0: Plants make their own food and have cellulose walls, not chitin.
whyNot.1: Protists are a mixed, mostly single-celled group; chitin walls and absorbing food mark a fungus.
whyNot.2: Animal cells have no cell walls, and animals ingest rather than absorb their food.

B.q: Which statement about the domain Archaea is accurate?
options: Its members are eukaryotes with a nucleus.
Its members are prokaryotes without peptidoglycan.
It is a kingdom within the domain Bacteria.
Its members are viruses that lack any cells.
B.why: Archaea are prokaryotes (no nucleus) that form their own domain; unlike bacteria, their walls contain no peptidoglycan.

whyNot.0: Eukaryotes with a nucleus make up the domain Eukarya, not Archaea.
whyNot.2: Archaea are a separate domain, not part of Bacteria.
whyNot.3: Archaea are living cells; viruses are not cells and are not in any domain.

B.q: After a meal, a person's body returns blood glucose to a narrow normal range. Which characteristic of life does this best illustrate?
B.why: Homeostasis is keeping internal conditions, such as blood glucose and body temperature, stable.

whyNot.1: Reproduction is making offspring, not keeping internal conditions steady.
whyNot.2: Growth and development is an increase in size and change in form over time.
whyNot.3: Evolution is a change in a population's inherited traits over generations, not a change within one person.

C.q: Organisms A and B share an order but belong to different families. Organisms A and C share a genus. Which statement is accurate?
options: A and B are more closely related than A and C.
A and B must also share the same genus.
A and C are more closely related than A and B.
A and C must also share the same species.
C.why: Genus is more specific than order. Organisms that share a genus also share family and order, so A and C are more closely related.

whyNot.0: Sharing only an order is a broader (looser) relationship than sharing a genus.
whyNot.1: A and B are in different families, so they cannot share a genus, which sits inside a family.
whyNot.3: Organisms in one genus can be different species (Canis lupus and Canis latrans).

C.q: A biologist studies how the deer, wolves and grasses of a national park interact with its soil and rainfall. Which level of organization is this?
C.why: An ecosystem is a community of organisms together with the nonliving environment, such as soil and rainfall.

whyNot.1: A community includes the living populations only; soil and rainfall make it an ecosystem.
whyNot.2: A population is one species, but this study includes deer, wolves and grasses.
whyNot.3: An organ system is a level inside one organism, such as the digestive system.

C.q: Which statement about viruses is accurate?
options: They are made of a single prokaryotic cell.
They reproduce only inside host cells.
They are classified in the domain Bacteria.
They carry out a metabolism of their own.
C.why: Viruses are not cells; they reproduce by taking over the machinery of a host cell.

whyNot.0: Viruses are not cells at all, prokaryotic or eukaryotic.
whyNot.2: The domains classify cellular life, so viruses are not placed in Bacteria.
whyNot.3: Viruses have no metabolism of their own; they use the host cell's.

reteach.title: A mailing address
reteach.question: Think of classification as a mailing address that narrows from a country down to one house. How does that map onto domain to species?

blocks.body: A letter is sorted by country, then state, city, ZIP code, street and house. Each step holds fewer homes and the homes inside it are closer together. Classification works the same way: a domain holds huge numbers of organisms, while a genus holds a few close relatives and a species is one kind of organism. Two people on the same street are closer neighbors than two people who only share a state, just as two species in one genus are closer relatives than two that share only an order.

blocks.text: On the envelope the last name comes first and gets a capital: Homo sapiens, never Homo Sapiens.

explain.body: Living things are made of cells, use energy, grow, reproduce, respond, keep homeostasis and carry DNA that is passed on. Nonliving things may show one feature (a crystal grows), but not the full set. Viruses have genetic material but are not cells and have no metabolism of their own.

test.q: Which feature of living things does a virus lack?
options: Genetic material such as DNA or RNA
Change in its genes over generations
A structure made of one or more cells
test.why: Viruses are not made of cells; that is why they sit outside the three domains.

whyNot.0: Viruses do carry genetic material, DNA or RNA.
whyNot.1: Viruses do change over generations as their genes mutate.
whyNot.3: Viruses have protein coats built from amino acids.

explain.body: Inside the body: atom, molecule, organelle, cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. Beyond it: population (one species), community (all species), ecosystem (community plus nonliving parts), biosphere (all ecosystems).

test.q: Which list runs from the smallest level of organization to the largest?
test.why: Organisms of one species form a population, and the populations in an area form a community.

whyNot.0: A population is made of organisms, so the organism comes first.
whyNot.1: A community is made of populations, so population comes before community.
whyNot.2: This runs from largest to smallest, the reverse of the order asked for.

explain.body: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. The binomial name is Genus species: in Homo sapiens, Homo is the genus and sapiens names the species within it.

test.q: In the scientific name Homo sapiens, what does the word Homo identify?
test.why: The first, capitalized word of a binomial name is the genus; the second names the species.

whyNot.0: The species is named by the second, lowercase word (sapiens).
whyNot.2: The family (Hominidae) is not part of the two-word name.
whyNot.3: The kingdom (Animalia) is not part of the two-word name.

explain.body: Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotes. Eukarya holds the protists, fungi (absorb food, chitin walls), plants (autotrophs, cellulose walls) and animals (heterotrophs, no walls).

test.q: Which pairing of kingdom and features is correct?
test.why: Plants make their own food by photosynthesis and build their cell walls from cellulose.

whyNot.0: Fungi are heterotrophs with chitin walls.
whyNot.2: Animal cells have no cell walls at all.
whyNot.3: Protists are eukaryotes with a nucleus.
